source_title: Since the mid-2000s, Patrick Stewart has worked with DV survivors and advocacy groups in his mother’s name
source_excerpt: Trigger warning: This article contains mentions of abuse and domestic violenceFor years, Sir Patrick Stewart worked with various organizations, non-profits, and other funding companies to help with issues across the world. However, his work with organizations helping domestic violence survivors remains the closest to his heart. For two decades, Sir Patrick Stewart served as a prominent male voice speaking out against domestic violence. Driven by the childhood memories of his fatherâs violence toward his mother, Gladys, Stewart turned his personal history into advocacy aimed at dismantling domestic abuse, reframing societal attitudes, and supporting victims.What motivated Patrick Stewart to work with domestic violence survivorsStewart grew up in Mirfield, Yorkshire, and from an early age, he grew up witnessing severe domestic abuse inflicted by his father, Alfred George Stewart, who had PTSD following his military enlistment. He was a Regimental Sergeant Major in World War II at the time, which heavily affected his behavior and temper. Over the years, Stewart was quite open about the horrors that he faced in his childhood.In an essay he wrote for The Guardian, Stewart wrote, âOur house was small, and when you grow up with domestic violence in a confined space, you learn to gauge, very precisely, the temperature of situations." I knew exactly when the shouting was done and a hand was about to be raisedâI also knew exactly when to insert a small body between the fist and her face, a skill no child should ever have to learn.âDuring a May 2013 Q&A panel at the Comicpalooza convention in Houston, Texas, one of the attendees named Heather Skye approached the mic to thank Stewart for his advocacy work with domestic violence charities. In his reply, the veteran actor detailed how his childhood had become the driving force for him to actually take action, bring some change in other peopleâs lives, and offer them a chance, even though he was never able to help his mother. He shared at the time, âAs a child, I heard in my home doctors and ambulance men say, 'Mrs. Stewart, you must have done something to provoke him.'" Mrs. Stewart, it takes two to make an argument. 'Wrong. Wrong! My mother did nothing to provoke that, and even if she hadâviolence is never ever a choice that a man should make... I do what I do in my mother's name, because I couldn't help her then. Now I can.âPatrick Stewartâs work with charities and non-profits to raise awareness about domestic violenceOver the years, the âExcaliburâ actor has worked with a lot of organizations to help domestic violence victims. He spearheaded Amnesty's "Stop Violence Against Women" campaign. In his essay âTurning the Tide,' which was published online on their official magazine website, he argued that domestic abuse is a public health epidemic and a human rights violation that thrives on male silence. He also added in his essay, "Violence against women diminishes us all. If you fail to raise your hand in protest, then you make yourself part of the problem.âLater, he officially became a patron and ambassador of one of the UK's leading domestic violence charities. He dedicated his work with the organization directly to his mother, regularly participating in fundraising campaigns and awareness events. According to the Refuge website, Stewart used his platform to lobby for legislative reform in the UK, contributing to the passage of the landmark Domestic Abuse Act 2021, which recognized children who witness domestic abuse as victims in their own right.Up until his passing, the veteran star was quite active and vocal about his advocacy and philanthropy.
